facts.claim: In the Small, Loewenstein, and Slovic study, the Rokia-only appeal averaged $2.38 while a statistics-only appeal averaged $1.14.
facts.mechanism: Because the constructed individual gave attention a single human target, participants could form an affective response more readily than from aggregate figures.
facts.commonError: The reported amounts prove that every individual story always raises exactly twice as much as any statistical appeal.
facts.whyWrong: They are means from one experimental design, and later work shows identifiable-victim effects vary with context and framing.

facts.claim: The Rokia experiment used a constructed 7-year-old girl from Mali rather than documenting a real named beneficiary.
facts.mechanism: Because identifiability was created inside controlled appeal text, the researchers could compare message framing without relying on a public person's biography.
facts.commonError: Rokia's personal history can be expanded as verified reportage about a real child.
facts.whyWrong: The figure was an experimental vignette, so adding scenes or biography would fabricate evidence.

facts.claim: The national truth campaign launched in early 2000 to discourage smoking among U.S. youth.
facts.mechanism: Because the campaign framed tobacco companies as manipulators, refusing cigarettes could express youthful independence rather than obedience to adult warnings.
facts.commonError: truth relied only on calm medical lectures delivered by tobacco executives.
facts.whyWrong: Its branded strategy used hard-hitting messages that challenged industry influence and recruited resistance.

facts.claim: A 2005 quasi-experimental evaluation estimated that truth accounted for about 22 percent of the 1999–2002 decline in youth smoking prevalence.
facts.mechanism: Because researchers related varying campaign exposure to prevalence trends in a large national student sample, they could estimate an exposure-associated contribution while controlling measured alternatives.
facts.commonError: The estimate means the campaign single-handedly caused the entire decline in youth smoking.
facts.whyWrong: The study attributed a portion of the decline and used an observational pre/post design, so the result is not total or randomized causation.

facts.claim: Floyd Lee brought 25 years of Marine Corps and Army cooking experience to the Pegasus dining facility near Baghdad airport.
facts.mechanism: Because he defined feeding soldiers as a morale mission, familiar supplies and routine service decisions were reorganized around emotional recovery.
facts.commonError: Pegasus succeeded only because Lee received a unique luxury-food supply unavailable to other facilities.
facts.whyWrong: The reported distinction was how standard resources were prepared and presented, guided by a different mission.

facts.claim: TxDOT has used Don't mess with Texas to mean don't litter since 1986.
facts.mechanism: Because the phrase made roadside cleanliness part of Texas pride, littering could feel inconsistent with the target audience's group identity.
facts.commonError: The phrase originated as a general state threat with no transportation or litter purpose.
facts.whyWrong: Its institutional origin was a state anti-litter effort, even though later popular use broadened the phrase.

facts.claim: An identity decision can be framed through who I am, what situation this is, and what someone like me does here.
facts.mechanism: Because group norms and self-concept supply behavioral defaults, the person need not calculate every consequence from scratch.
facts.commonError: Identity appeals work only by offering a direct cash reward to the audience.
facts.whyWrong: Cash belongs to narrow consequence-based self-interest; identity works through role and norm consistency.

facts.claim: WIIFY means What's In It For You, but the relevant benefit can include meaning, belonging, mastery, or pride.
facts.mechanism: Because people value psychological and social outcomes as well as material gain, a message can connect action to higher-order motives.
facts.commonError: WIIFY requires reducing every appeal to price, pay, or personal convenience.
facts.whyWrong: That narrow reading misses motives such as service identity and collective pride that can be more powerful than money.

facts.claim: Semantic stretch weakens an emotional association when a valued word is applied to many weakly related things.
facts.mechanism: Because repeated loose use makes the label less diagnostic of the original value, audiences stop feeling the intended association.
facts.commonError: Using a powerful value word in every message continuously strengthens its emotional force.
facts.whyWrong: Overextension dilutes the word's specificity and can make the appeal sound empty or promotional.
